**CAPACITY DEPLOYMENT AND FUNDING IN FOCUS**. Tal Liani remains constructive on CoreWeave despite recent volatility across AI infrastructure, with the core thesis supported by significant contracted demand and a strong data center pipeline. CoreWeave’s RPO stood at ~$129bn as of early 3Q26, but converting that backlog into revenue depends on continued capacity deployment and access to capital. Into the print, Tal is focused on capacity additions, potential operating-margin upside, funding requirements and capex. He reiterates Buy and a $140 PO.
  * **KEY METRICS: ACTIVE POWER, REVENUE AND MARGINS**. CoreWeave brought 500MW online in 2Q26, and Tal expects another 200MW in 3Q26, taking total active power to 1.7GW. He models 3Q26 revenue of ~$3.65bn, up 168% YoY and ~3% above Street, with operating margin of 6.7% versus Street at 6.9%. Recently deployed capacity and increasing revenue scale could support upside to profitability, while continued execution on infrastructure deployment remains critical to the growth outlook. Longer term, Tal expects CoreWeave to add 1.4-1.5GW annually over each of the next three years, supporting revenue growth of 152%/105%/63% in FY26/FY27/FY28.
  * **CAPEX / FUNDING: HOW DOES COREWEAVE FUND THE BUILDOUT**? Funding remains the central debate given the infrastructure required to convert ~$129bn of RPO into revenue. Tal estimates CoreWeave needs ~$20bn of additional funding and will look for greater clarity around financing options, the cost of debt given recent credit-spread widening, and management’s preference for debt versus equity. He models 3Q26 capex of $12.5bn, up 558% YoY and broadly in line with Street, and FY26 capex of ~$37.0bn. Greater visibility into funding costs and capital availability would be important for confidence that CoreWeave can execute against its contracted demand without constraining the capacity ramp.

The spike in bond yields into the high-15% area overstates concerns that CRWV will lose access to capital needed to fund its contracted growth.****

** **

  * **HY bonds yields are not representative of the true marginal funding cost.** CRWV’s primary GPU financing remains SPV-level secured loans, which amortize over the underlying customer contracts. Early loans are already being repaid, secondary loan prices have held up better, and IG customer contracts should support additional IG-rated financings. Customer prepayments and vendor financing provide further options.

source.narrative_excerpt:
**The debate is increasingly fundamentals vs. forced liquidation**. Conversations with senior investors were strikingly split. On one side, the magnitude and speed of the move increasingly feels technical/liquidation-driven, with HF shutdowns, gross reductions and forced deleveraging potentially amplifying the selloff. At the same time, several investors think the market is now discounting an extreme deterioration in AI earnings that isn't yet visible in fundamentals. Recent hyperscaler results, supplier commentary and the lack of evidence of meaningful DC cancellations/backlog deterioration were repeatedly cited as reasons the underlying AI picture looks considerably better than the tape. That said, even constructive investors are not rushing to call the bottom or put substantial risk back on yet.
  * **The more legitimate bear case is shifting from “AI doesn't work” to financing, Lab growth and durability of the build**. The AI infrastructure cycle requires enormous amounts of capital, while the cost of both debt and equity has risen materially. The concern is that tighter capital eventually constrains Lab/neocloud spending, training demand and therefore semis/memory. Lab ARR is emerging as one of the key KPIs investors want to see accelerate meaningfully. Several investors think 2027 remains relatively protected and 2028+ is the bigger sustainability question, although the harder bear case is that financing constraints ultimately drive meaningful 2027 earnings revisions.
  * **At the same time, valuations are creating some pretty extreme asymmetries**. One investor buying DRAM into the selloff cited roughly 1.5x 2029 P/E, essentially asking what level of earnings collapse is now being discounted. The framework is simple: if earnings eventually fall >90%, some stocks could still prove expensive; if they don't, parts of the group are getting exceptionally cheap. Others are looking specifically for names where several years of AI earnings appear to have been largely discounted away. # Datadog

## CEO and CFO Investor Call Takeaways

  
---  
  
By Samik Chatterjee, CFA
AC,
Jaiden R
Patel,
Mashu
Nishi

Click here for the full document and
disclaimers

| Overweight

DDOG, DDOG US  
Price (05 Nov 26):$174.60  
  
We hosted an investor call with CEO Olivier Pomel and CFO David Obstler
following F3Q earnings, where we had the opportunity to discuss emerging
business trends for Datadog, particularly around resilience of growth dynamics
between the different customer cohorts (core, non-AI native, largest
customer), approach to guidance philosophy, the increasing importance of
Observability from AI agents, among other major business topics. Key takeaways
from the discussion included:

  * AI agents could reinforce the strategic importance of Observability rather than displace it. Addressing the longer-term risk that AI agents and general-purpose LLMs could eventually perform observability and remediation themselves, Datadog argued that the underlying workloads require a fundamentally different technical and economic approach. Unlike general-purpose LLMs, observability involves continuously processing massive volumes of specialized telemetry, including logs, metrics, traces, and topology data, which require different model architectures and performance characteristics. Datadog’s access to production data, critical customer workflows, and specialized tooling creates a differentiated position to develop these capabilities. The company suggested that observability could ultimately become one of the last responsibilities requiring human oversight, supporting the platform’s relevance as software environments become increasingly autonomous.
  * Core business acceleration is broad-based, supported by multiple growth drivers. Building on the acceleration in non-AI customer revenue growth highlighted in the F3Q earnings print, management expressed confidence in the demand environment, pointing to a combination of successful sales capacity expansion, platform consolidation, broader product adoption, and market share gains. Non-AI natives are increasingly migrating to the cloud, adopting additional Datadog products, and growing their usage. The company provided additional context on moderating customer additions, noting that Datadog typically adds approximately 2K gross new logos per quarter, with gross new logos influenced by fluctuations among small customers and expanded credits. Datadog has broadened its startup program and is allocating more engineering resources to high-growth startups, and startup credits can temporarily reduce logo additions.
  * Model agnosticism is not the objective, with Datadog prioritizing performance, economics, and differentiation. The company aims to utilize the models best suited to individual workloads based on performance, cost efficiency, and differentiation. Datadog expects to maintain a mix of commercial frontier models, open-weight models, and proprietary models, with specialized offerings such as Scout demonstrating the potential to achieve superior economics and performance for observability-specific use cases. The database market illustrates how enterprises combine commercial, open-source, and internally developed technologies, a pattern likely to extend to AI, with proprietary models used where specialized performance or economics create differentiation and off-the-shelf offerings serving more general use cases.
  * Logs unbundling is more about addressing structural data growth than defending against lower-cost competitors. Customers typically experience an orders-of-magnitude growth in log volumes while their underlying businesses expand at far more modest rates, thus making proportional increases in log management spending economically unsustainable. Management outlined three approaches to addressing this dynamic: 1) more selective data collection and retention, including sampling, 2) tailoring log capabilities and pricing to specific use cases through unbundling, and 3) continued engineering innovation to process and retain more data at lower costs. Longer term, these initiatives should allow Datadog to capture a greater share of customer workloads and wallet share.
  * Guidance philosophy remains unchanged, with Datadog emphasizing conservatism around consumption trends. Datadog reiterated that the company’s forecasting approach incorporates recent consumption trends and net retention rates, discounted for usage volatility and its historical beat-and-raise cadence. With respect to F3Q, the ~$47M revenue beat vs. guidance of $1.14B at the mid-point was split roughly 60/40 between the core business and Datadog’s largest customer. As for the F4Q guidance, management reiterated that the guide assumes only the largest customer’s minimum contractual commitment which would be a sequential headwind given the large customer consumer materially above the minimum commit in F3Q. For 2027, Datadog expects to continue modeling that customer at contractual minimums (only until current contract expiry, without assuming renewal in guidance until the contract is renewed) and other AI-native customers using risk-adjusted consumption trends.
  * Margin framework remains intact, with AI changing the composition of R&D investments. Gross margins of around 80% are sustainable with quarterly fluctuations reflecting the timing and benefits of engineering projects rather than volume-based discounts associated with larger customer commitments. On PF operating margins, Datadog’s consumption-based model provides natural operating leverage, as margins typically expand when revenue accelerates because costs do not increase at the same pace, creating opportunities to reinvest in areas around go-to-market and AI development, while maintaining its existing long-term margin framework. The composition of R&D spend, which has historically represented approximately 30% of revenue, is increasingly shifting from personnel toward technology, AI inference, and tokens, while not changing the overall investment envelope. On capital allocation, management reiterated its disciplined approach to M&A, with acquisitions focused on talent, TAM expansion, and product acceleration; share repurchases could eventually become an alternative if cash continues to accumulate.
